<div class="clt-lesson batch-lesson" data-lesson="chi"><h2 id="learning-goals">What are we trying to understand?</h2><p><strong>How different are observed counts from the counts we would expect under a null model?</strong></p><p>Return to the workshop example from conditional probability. Now imagine the counts are a sample of 100 independent observations rather than a known population. Compare a test of independence with a goodness-of-fit test against specified category proportions.</p><div class="clt-overview"><strong>Learning goals</strong><ol><li>Compute expected counts under the null.</li><li>Explain how each cell contributes to the chi-square statistic.</li><li>Distinguish independence and goodness-of-fit questions.</li><li>Interpret the p-value and expected-count condition.</li></ol></div><h2 id="explore">Make a prediction and explore</h2><section class="clt-simulator"><p>Predict which setting produces χ² = 0.</p><div class="controls"><div><label for="mode">Research question</label><select id="mode"><option value="ind">Independence (2 × 2 table)</option><option value="gof">Goodness of fit (three categories)</option></select></div><div><label for="shift"><span id="shift-label">Students in both categories</span>: <output id="shift-v">30</output></label><input id="shift" type="range" min="0" max="40" step="1" value="30"></div></div><p id="null"></p><div class="metrics"><div class="metric"><span>χ² statistic</span><strong id="chi">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>Degrees of freedom</span><strong id="df">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>p-value</span><strong id="p">—</strong></div></div><div id="chart" class="plot"></div><p class="note">Dark bars: observed. Light bars: expected under H₀. Counts are also shown below.</p><table class="data-table"><caption>Cell-by-cell comparison</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Category</th><th scope="col">Observed</th><th scope="col">Expected</th><th scope="col">Contribution</th></tr></thead><tbody id="chi-table"></tbody></table><p id="decision" role="status"></p><p class="note">Expected counts are at least 20 in both scenarios. Illustrative tables are constructed, not actual research findings.</p></section><h2 id="interpret">Interpret what you find</h2><ol><li>Select independence and set the overlap to 20. Verify every observed count equals its expected count.</li><li>Compare overlap 10 and 30. Why are the chi-square statistics equal?</li><li>Select goodness of fit, set the shift to zero, then move away from zero. Identify the largest cell contribution.</li><li>Explain why independence is a population hypothesis and why a finite sample need not match expected counts exactly.</li></ol><h2 id="explanation">What is the method telling us?</h2><div class="formula">χ² = Σ (observed − expected)² / expected<br>Independence: expected = row total × column total / grand total; df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1)<br>Goodness of fit: expected = n × hypothesized category probability; df = categories − 1 when probabilities are fully specified</div><p>The chi-square statistic is nonnegative and uses the upper tail. A large discrepancy is evidence against the null, not proof of causation. The usual chi-square approximation assumes independent observations and sufficiently large expected counts (a common introductory rule is at least five per cell). Goodness of fit compares one variable with a specified distribution; independence compares two categorical variables.</p><h2 id="knowledge-check">Check your understanding</h2><p>Choose an answer, then check your reasoning.
